title: Biotechnology & Genetic Engineering
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 400L Biotechnology and Genetic Engineering curriculum: recombinant DNA technology, cloning vectors, PCR and sequencing, gene expression systems, blotting techniques, CRISPR gene editing, and applications in medicine, agriculture and industry, building on 200-300L molecular biology and biochemistry.

questions.question: Restriction endonucleases used in recombinant DNA technology recognize and cleave DNA at specific sequences called:
questions.correct_answer: Palindromic recognition sites
questions.explanation: Most type II restriction enzymes recognize short palindromic (reverse-complement symmetric) DNA sequences, such as EcoRI's GAATTC, and cleave both strands at defined positions within or near this site.

questions.question: Restriction enzymes that cleave DNA to leave short single-stranded overhangs, useful for directional cloning, produce what are called:
questions.correct_answer: Sticky ends
questions.explanation: Enzymes like EcoRI cut asymmetrically within the recognition site, generating complementary single-stranded overhangs (sticky ends) that can base-pair with compatible ends for efficient ligation.

questions.question: Which enzyme is used to covalently join the sugar-phosphate backbones of DNA fragments after restriction digestion and annealing during cloning?
questions.correct_answer: DNA ligase
questions.explanation: DNA ligase catalyzes the formation of a phosphodiester bond between adjacent 3'-OH and 5'-phosphate ends, sealing nicks to covalently join a DNA insert into a vector.

questions.question: Plasmid cloning vectors typically carry which two essential features for propagation and screening in bacterial hosts?
options: An origin of replication and a selectable marker gene
A promoter for RNA polymerase II only
questions.correct_answer: An origin of replication and a selectable marker gene
questions.explanation: A plasmid vector needs an origin of replication to be maintained and copied within the host bacterium, and a selectable marker (commonly antibiotic resistance) to allow identification of transformed cells.

questions.question: Compared to plasmids, bacteriophage lambda vectors are advantageous for constructing genomic libraries mainly because they:
options: Can accommodate larger DNA inserts and package/infect host cells with high efficiency
Replicate independently of the host chromosome only in eukaryotes
Cannot be propagated in E. coli
questions.correct_answer: Can accommodate larger DNA inserts and package/infect host cells with high efficiency
questions.explanation: Lambda phage vectors tolerate larger inserts than standard plasmids and use highly efficient in vitro packaging and phage infection to introduce DNA into host cells, making them well suited for genomic libraries.

questions.question: Cosmid and BAC (bacterial artificial chromosome) vectors were developed primarily to:
options: Clone very large DNA fragments (tens to hundreds of kilobases)
Express proteins at very high levels in mammalian cells
Replace the need for restriction enzymes in cloning
Enable cloning without a bacterial host
questions.correct_answer: Clone very large DNA fragments (tens to hundreds of kilobases)
questions.explanation: Cosmids (using lambda cos sites in a plasmid backbone) and BACs (based on the F-factor) were designed to stably carry much larger inserts than standard plasmids, essential for genome mapping and sequencing projects.

questions.question: In the polymerase chain reaction (PCR), the enzyme Taq polymerase is prized for its ability to:
options: Remain active after repeated exposure to high denaturation temperatures
Proofread and correct all misincorporated bases
Synthesize DNA in the absence of primers
questions.correct_answer: Remain active after repeated exposure to high denaturation temperatures
questions.explanation: Taq polymerase, isolated from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus, is heat-stable and survives the ~95C denaturation step repeated in each PCR cycle, unlike typical mesophilic polymerases.

questions.question: The three repeated steps of a standard PCR cycle, in order, are:
questions.correct_answer: Denaturation, annealing, extension
questions.explanation: Each PCR cycle denatures the double-stranded template (heat), anneals short primers to the single strands (cooling), and extends new DNA strands from the primers using thermostable polymerase.

questions.question: Reverse transcriptase-PCR (RT-PCR) is used to amplify and study gene expression by first converting which template into complementary DNA (cDNA)?
questions.correct_answer: mRNA
questions.explanation: Reverse transcriptase synthesizes single-stranded cDNA using mRNA as a template, and this cDNA (lacking introns) can then be PCR-amplified to study or clone expressed genes.

questions.question: Sanger (chain-termination) DNA sequencing relies on the incorporation of which type of nucleotide analog to randomly halt DNA synthesis at each position?
questions.correct_answer: Dideoxynucleotides (ddNTPs) lacking a 3'-OH group
questions.explanation: ddNTPs lack the 3'-hydroxyl needed to form the next phosphodiester bond, so their random incorporation during in vitro DNA synthesis terminates chain elongation, producing fragments of varying length that reveal the sequence.

questions.question: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) platforms differ fundamentally from Sanger sequencing mainly by:
options: Sequencing millions of DNA fragments simultaneously (massively parallel sequencing)
Requiring radioactive labeling of every nucleotide
Eliminating the need for a DNA polymerase
questions.correct_answer: Sequencing millions of DNA fragments simultaneously (massively parallel sequencing)
questions.explanation: NGS technologies achieve massively parallel sequencing of millions of clonally amplified DNA fragments at once, dramatically increasing throughput and lowering cost compared to the one-fragment-at-a-time Sanger method.

questions.question: A genomic DNA library differs from a cDNA library in that a genomic library contains:
options: Both coding (exon) and non-coding (intron/regulatory) sequences from the entire genome
Only sequences that are actively expressed as mRNA
Only fully processed, intron-free coding sequences
questions.correct_answer: Both coding (exon) and non-coding (intron/regulatory) sequences from the entire genome
questions.explanation: A genomic library is made directly from an organism's genomic DNA and thus includes introns, promoters, and intergenic regions, whereas a cDNA library reflects only the spliced, expressed mRNA sequences of the tissue it was made from.

questions.question: Southern blotting is a molecular technique used to detect specific sequences of which molecule?
questions.correct_answer: DNA
questions.explanation: Southern blotting transfers electrophoresed DNA fragments onto a membrane and probes them with a labeled complementary sequence, allowing detection of specific DNA sequences (e.g., in restriction fragment length analysis).

questions.question: Northern blotting is analogous to Southern blotting but is used to detect and analyze:
questions.correct_answer: RNA transcripts
questions.explanation: Northern blotting separates RNA by electrophoresis, transfers it to a membrane, and hybridizes it with a labeled probe, allowing researchers to detect and estimate the size/abundance of specific mRNA transcripts.

questions.question: Western blotting identifies specific proteins in a complex mixture primarily using:
options: Specific antibodies against the target protein
questions.correct_answer: Specific antibodies against the target protein
questions.explanation: After separating proteins by SDS-PAGE and transferring them to a membrane, Western blotting uses a primary antibody specific to the target protein, followed by a labeled secondary antibody, for detection.

questions.question: In the CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing system, the guide RNA (gRNA) functions to:
options: Direct the Cas9 nuclease to a specific complementary genomic DNA sequence
Provide the energy for DNA cleavage
Repair the double-strand break after cutting
Serve as the template for homologous recombination in all cases
questions.correct_answer: Direct the Cas9 nuclease to a specific complementary genomic DNA sequence
questions.explanation: The guide RNA base-pairs with a complementary target DNA sequence, positioning the Cas9 nuclease to introduce a double-strand break at that specific genomic locus.

questions.question: Cas9-mediated DNA cleavage requires recognition of a short sequence immediately adjacent to the target site called the:
questions.correct_answer: PAM (protospacer adjacent motif)
questions.explanation: Cas9 will only cleave DNA if the target sequence is immediately followed by a PAM sequence (commonly 5'-NGG-3' for Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9), which the enzyme uses to license cleavage and avoid self-targeting.

questions.question: After a CRISPR-Cas9-induced double-strand break, precise insertion of a desired sequence (knock-in) is typically achieved by exploiting which cellular repair pathway with a supplied donor template?
questions.correct_answer: Homology-directed repair (HDR)
questions.explanation: Supplying a donor DNA template with homology arms flanking the break allows the cell's HDR machinery to copy the desired sequence into the genome precisely, unlike error-prone NHEJ which is typically used for gene disruption.

questions.question: Bacterial transformation with a recombinant plasmid is commonly enhanced in the laboratory by which treatment?
options: Heat shock of calcium chloride-treated competent cells
Freezing the plasmid DNA in liquid nitrogen without cells
questions.correct_answer: Heat shock of calcium chloride-treated competent cells
questions.explanation: CaCl2 treatment renders bacterial cell membranes permeable to DNA, and a brief heat shock (e.g., 42C) creates a thermal imbalance that drives plasmid DNA uptake into the competent cells.

questions.question: Electroporation as a gene delivery method works by:
options: Using a brief electrical pulse to transiently create pores in the cell membrane for DNA entry
Coating DNA onto gold particles fired into cells
Packaging DNA into a viral capsid for infection
Using lipid vesicles to fuse with the cell membrane
questions.correct_answer: Using a brief electrical pulse to transiently create pores in the cell membrane for DNA entry
questions.explanation: Electroporation applies a short, high-voltage electrical pulse that destabilizes the lipid bilayer, creating transient pores through which DNA (or other molecules) can enter the cell before the membrane reseals.

questions.question: Which expression host is most commonly used for large-scale, low-cost production of simple recombinant proteins that do not require extensive post-translational modification?
questions.correct_answer: Escherichia coli
questions.explanation: E. coli is fast-growing, genetically well-characterized, and inexpensive to culture, making it the default host for producing simple recombinant proteins such as insulin, though it cannot perform complex eukaryotic glycosylation.

questions.question: Recombinant proteins requiring proper eukaryotic post-translational modifications such as glycosylation are typically produced using which expression system?
options: Mammalian cell lines (e.g., CHO cells) or yeast
questions.correct_answer: Mammalian cell lines (e.g., CHO cells) or yeast
questions.explanation: Mammalian cells (and, to a lesser extent, yeast) possess the enzymatic machinery for complex glycosylation and other post-translational modifications needed for the correct folding and function of many therapeutic proteins, which bacteria lack.

questions.question: Recombinant human insulin, one of the first biotechnology products, was originally produced by expressing the A and B chains separately in which host organism before combining them?
questions.correct_answer: Escherichia coli
questions.explanation: The pioneering recombinant insulin product (Humulin) was made by separately expressing the insulin A and B chains as fusion proteins in E. coli, then chemically combining and folding them via disulfide bond formation.

questions.question: Monoclonal antibodies are traditionally produced by fusing an antibody-producing B lymphocyte with a myeloma cell to create a:
questions.correct_answer: Hybridoma
questions.explanation: Hybridoma technology (Kohler and Milstein) fuses a short-lived, antibody-secreting B cell with an immortal myeloma cell, yielding a hybridoma that both proliferates indefinitely and secretes a single, defined (monoclonal) antibody.

questions.question: In gene therapy, viral vectors such as modified adenoviruses or lentiviruses are commonly used because they:
options: Naturally and efficiently deliver genetic material into host cells
Replicate independently of a host genome after packaging
Always integrate randomly and cause no safety concerns
questions.correct_answer: Naturally and efficiently deliver genetic material into host cells
questions.explanation: Viruses have evolved highly efficient mechanisms for entering cells and delivering their genetic material; gene therapy exploits this by replacing viral genes with a therapeutic gene while retaining the delivery machinery.

questions.question: A key safety distinction in gene therapy vectors is that integrating vectors (e.g., retroviruses) carry a risk of insertional mutagenesis, whereas non-integrating vectors such as adeno-associated virus (AAV) mainly:
options: Persist as episomes without inserting into the host chromosome
Always cause permanent, heritable germline changes
Cannot express their transgene at all
Replicate uncontrollably within the host cell
questions.correct_answer: Persist as episomes without inserting into the host chromosome
questions.explanation: AAV vectors largely remain as extrachromosomal episomes rather than integrating into the host genome, reducing (though not eliminating) the risk of insertional mutagenesis compared to integrating retroviral/lentiviral vectors.

questions.question: Transgenic plants engineered to express the Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) toxin gene are valued agriculturally because the toxin:
options: Confers resistance to specific insect pests by disrupting their gut epithelium
Increases the plant's photosynthetic rate directly
Fixes atmospheric nitrogen for the plant
questions.correct_answer: Confers resistance to specific insect pests by disrupting their gut epithelium
questions.explanation: Bt delta-endotoxin is selectively toxic to certain insect larvae; upon ingestion it binds gut epithelial receptors and forms pores that lyse gut cells, killing the pest while being harmless to mammals, hence its use in insect-resistant GM crops.

questions.question: Agrobacterium tumefaciens is widely used as a natural vector for plant genetic engineering because it can transfer a segment of its Ti plasmid, called T-DNA, directly into:
options: The plant cell's chloroplast genome only
The plant cell wall as a structural component
questions.correct_answer: The plant cell's nuclear genome
questions.explanation: Agrobacterium naturally transfers and integrates T-DNA from its tumor-inducing (Ti) plasmid into the plant nuclear genome; biotechnologists replace the oncogenic T-DNA genes with genes of interest for stable plant transformation.

questions.question: Bioinformatics tools such as BLAST (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool) are used in biotechnology primarily to:
options: Compare a query DNA or protein sequence against databases to find similar sequences
Replace the need for PCR amplification
questions.correct_answer: Compare a query DNA or protein sequence against databases to find similar sequences
questions.explanation: BLAST algorithmically searches sequence databases for regions of local similarity to a query sequence, helping researchers identify gene function, homologs, and evolutionary relationships.

questions.question: In an expression vector for recombinant protein production, the promoter sequence functions to:
options: Direct RNA polymerase to initiate transcription of the downstream gene
Terminate translation at the correct codon
Encode the selectable antibiotic resistance marker
questions.correct_answer: Direct RNA polymerase to initiate transcription of the downstream gene
questions.explanation: The promoter is the DNA sequence recognized by RNA polymerase (often with associated transcription factors) that determines where and how strongly transcription of the cloned gene begins.

questions.question: A major ethical and biosafety concern specifically associated with germline gene editing (as opposed to somatic gene editing) is that induced changes:
options: Are heritable and passed on to future generations
Only affect a single treated individual temporarily
Cannot be detected by any sequencing method
Are automatically reversed after one generation
questions.correct_answer: Are heritable and passed on to future generations
questions.explanation: Because germline editing alters the DNA of reproductive cells or embryos, any changes (intended or off-target) become heritable and can be transmitted to offspring, raising unique ethical concerns not present with somatic cell editing.

questions.question: Site-directed mutagenesis is a technique used to introduce a specific, defined change at a chosen position in a cloned gene, most commonly for the purpose of:
options: Studying the functional role of a specific amino acid residue in a protein
Sequencing an entire genome de novo
Fusing two unrelated organisms' entire genomes
questions.correct_answer: Studying the functional role of a specific amino acid residue in a protein
questions.explanation: By precisely changing a codon (e.g., via PCR-based mutagenesis) and expressing the mutant protein, researchers can directly test the contribution of a specific amino acid to enzyme catalysis, binding, or stability.

questions.question: A recombinant protein expressed in E. coli is often fused to a polyhistidine (His) tag mainly to facilitate:
options: Purification by immobilized metal affinity chromatography
Increased transcription rate of the gene
Secretion into the culture medium in all cases
questions.correct_answer: Purification by immobilized metal affinity chromatography
questions.explanation: A His-tag binds with high affinity to immobilized divalent metal ions (e.g., Ni2+) on a chromatography resin, allowing the tagged recombinant protein to be selectively captured and purified from a complex cell lysate.
